title: Truth, not custom, must govern veiling
english: I have now taken up the cause of my own view, and I will show in Latin as well that our virgins ought to be veiled from the moment they have passed into womanhood. Truth demands this, and no one can set limits to truth: not the passage of time, not the patronage of important persons, not the privilege of any region. For it is from these things that custom generally takes its beginning. Born from some ignorance or simplicity, custom is strengthened into use by succession, and in this way it asserts its claim against truth.

But our Lord Christ named himself truth, not custom. If Christ is always, and prior to all things, then truth is equally everlasting and ancient. Let those to whom what is old seems new look to it. It is not so much novelty as truth that refutes heresies. Whatever savors against truth will be heresy, even if it is an old custom. Besides, if anyone is ignorant of something, that is his own fault. What is unknown ought to be sought out just as much as what is known ought to be received.

The rule of faith is indeed altogether one, alone immovable and unreformable: namely, to believe in one God almighty, maker of the world, and in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised from the dead on the third day, received into heaven, now seated at the right hand of the Father, coming to judge the living and the dead through the resurrection of the flesh as well. While this law of faith remains, everything else of discipline and conduct admits the novelty of correction, as the grace of God works and advances even to the end.

For what kind of thing is it that, while the devil is always working and adding daily to the devices of wickedness, the work of God should either have ceased or stopped advancing? The Lord sent the Holy Spirit for this very reason: because human limitation could not grasp everything at once, discipline should be gradually directed, ordered, and brought to perfection by the Holy Spirit, who acts in the Lord's place. He says, "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; when that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth and will announce to you the things that are coming" (John 16:12-13). But he also declared this work of his above.

What then is the administration of the Holy Spirit except this: that discipline is directed, that Scriptures are revealed, that understanding is reformed, that progress is made toward better things? Nothing is without its act; all things await their time. Finally Ecclesiastes says, "There is a time for every matter" (Ecclesiastes 3:1). Look at creation itself: it is advanced gradually toward fruit. First there is a grain, and from the grain a shoot arises, and from the shoot a little tree struggles forth. Then branches and leaves grow strong, and the whole name of tree is spread out; then the swelling of the bud comes, and the flower is released from the bud, and from the flower the fruit is opened. This too, for some time rough and unformed, gradually directing its own age, is trained into the gentleness of flavor.

So also righteousness, for the same God is God of righteousness and of creation, was at first in its rudiments, fearing God by nature; then through the law and the prophets it advanced into infancy; then through the gospel it boiled over into youth; now through the Holy Spirit it is composed into maturity. He alone will be the teacher from Christ, to be named and revered. For he does not speak from himself, but what is commanded by Christ. He alone is the forerunner, because he alone comes after Christ. Those who have received him set truth before custom. Those who have heard him prophesying until now, not long ago, cover their virgins.
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by stating his thesis that virgins must be veiled once they reach maturity, and begins arguing that truth, not custom, must rule church discipline.

title: Custom on both sides, but the veiling custom is the one to choose
english: But for now I do not want to count this custom as truth. Let it remain custom for the time being, so that I may set custom against custom. Throughout Greece and certain barbarian parts of it, many churches hide their virgins. This practice exists somewhere under our own sky too, so that no one can ascribe that custom to Greek or barbarian gentile ways. But I have put forward those churches which the apostles themselves or apostolic men founded, and I think before certain others. They have the same authority of custom, and they plead their times and predecessors more than these later churches of ours do. What shall we observe? What shall we choose? We cannot reject a custom we cannot condemn, since it is not foreign, because it belongs not to foreigners, with whom we share the bond of peace and the name of brotherhood. We and they have one faith, one God, the same Christ, the same hope, the same sacraments of baptism. Let me say it once: we are one church. So whatever belongs to our people belongs to us. Otherwise you divide the body.

Yet here, as is usually done in all matters variously established and doubtful and uncertain, an examination should have been applied: which of two such different customs better befits the discipline of God. And certainly the one to be chosen is the one that encloses virgins, known to God alone. For them, besides the fact that glory is to be sought from God and not from human beings, even their own good is to be blushed at. You would confound a virgin more by praising her than by criticizing her, because the forehead of sin is harder, taught shamelessness by sin itself and in sin itself. For no one would have approved that custom which denies virgins while it displays them, except people just like the virgins themselves. For the kind of eyes that want a virgin to be seen are the kind a virgin has who wants to be seen. The same kinds of eyes desire each other. It belongs to the same lust to be seen and to see. It is as much the mark of a holy man to blush if he has seen a virgin as it is of a holy virgin if she has been seen by a man.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the claim that veiling virgins is only a local custom, by pointing to older churches founded by apostles that also veil virgins, and then arguing that the veiling custom is the one that befits God's discipline.

title: Truth must break out against custom
english: But those most holy predecessors of ours did not even want to examine the customs. Still, among us until very recently both customs were shared in with some tolerance. The matter was left to each person's choice, so that any woman could either be veiled or be displayed, just as she could marry—which itself is neither forced nor forbidden. Truth was content to make a pact with custom, so that under custom's name it could quietly enjoy itself, at least in part. But once knowledge began to advance, so that through the freedom of both practices the evidence of the better part might emerge, immediately that enemy of good things and of so many good institutions did his work. Virgins devoted to men compete against virgins of God, stirred up to reckless boldness with completely bare foreheads, and they are considered virgins who can ask something from men—let alone such a deed as this, that God's virgins, who are all the more free because they are servants of Christ alone, should be handed over to their rivals. "We are scandalized," they say, "because others walk about differently," and they prefer to be scandalized than to be provoked. Scandal, unless I am mistaken, is not the example of a good thing but of an evil thing, building toward sin. Good things scandalize no one except a bad mind. If modesty is good, and shamefastness, and contempt for glory, seeking to please God alone, then let those who are scandalized by such a good recognize their own evil. What if the incontinent were to say they are scandalized by the continent—should continence be called back? And so that the repeatedly married are not scandalized, must monogamy be rejected? Why do these women not rather complain that wantonness and the shamelessness of virginity put on display are a scandal to them? It is because of such heads put on display, then, that holy virgins are dragged into the church, blushing because they are recognized in the midst, trembling because they are uncovered when summoned, as if to defilement. For this too they do not want to suffer. Every public display of a good virgin is a form of defilement, and yet suffering violence to the flesh is less, because it comes from the working of nature. But when the spirit itself is violated in a virgin by the removal of her veil, she has learned to lose what she was protecting. O sacrilegious hands, which have been able to strip off a garment dedicated to God! What worse could any persecutor have done, if he had known this was chosen by a virgin? You have uncovered a girl from her head, and now the whole virgin is no longer herself; she has become another. Rise up, then, truth—rise up and burst forth as if from patience! I do not want you to defend any custom; for even that custom under which you were enjoying yourself is now being attacked. Show that you are the one who veils virgins. Interpret your own Scriptures yourself, which custom does not know. For if it had known them, it would never have existed.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing the church's past tolerance of both veiled and unveiled virgins, and now turns to rebuke those who are scandalized by the better practice.

title: Woman Already Includes Virgin
english: Custom argues from Scripture against truth, as it always does. Our opponents meet us at once with this objection. They say the apostle makes no mention of virgins where he lays down the veil. He names only women. If he had wanted virgins to be veiled, they say, he would have spoken of virgins by name alongside women. He does just that elsewhere. Where he treats marriage, he also declares what virgins must observe.

So they claim virgins are not held by the law of veiling the head. The law does not name them, so it does not command them. Indeed, they say, this leaves them unveiled, since those who are not even named are not commanded. We turn the same argument back on them. The apostle knew how to name each kind separately elsewhere, virgin and woman, that is, a woman who is not a virgin. He drew that distinction when he needed it. Where he does not name the virgin, he drops the distinction on purpose. His silence proves sharing of condition. He could have set virgin apart from woman here as well.

He says elsewhere, "Woman and virgin are divided." So those he did not divide by his silence, he joined. Some think that division helps them here. It does not. What is said elsewhere has no force where it is not said, unless the cause is the same elsewhere, so that saying it once is enough. But the cause that divides virgin and woman there lies far from this case. The apostle says, "The unmarried — that is, the virgin — cares for the things of the Lord, so she may be holy in body and in spirit, but the married — that is, a woman who is not a virgin — cares how to please her husband" (1 Corinthians 7:34). That explains the division there. It has no place in this chapter. Here he pronounces nothing about marriage, nor about the mind and thoughts of woman and virgin. He speaks only about veiling the head. The Holy Spirit wanted no dispute about this. He willed the virgin to be understood under the one name of woman. He did not separate her by naming her apart from woman, and by not separating her he joined her to the woman from whom he did not separate her.

Is it strange now to use the leading word and still mean all the rest under that word, when there is no need to spell out each part of the whole? Short speech is both welcome and needed by nature. Long, wordy speech is burdensome and empty. So we rest content with general words, which hold the lesser kinds inside themselves. Take the word itself. Female is the word of nature. Woman is the general form of that word of nature. Under that general term come the special terms, virgin or married or widow, with as many names of age as join them. The special rests under the general, for the general comes first, the later follows the earlier, and the part belongs to the whole. What is subject to it is understood in it and meant in it, because it is held in it. When you name the body, you need not name each limb, neither hand nor foot nor any other part. If you say world, heaven is there with all it holds, sun and moon and stars, earth and seas, and every kind of element. You have named them all when you name what holds them all. So in naming woman he has named whatever belongs to woman.
orientation: Tertullian answers the objection that the apostle ordered only women and not virgins to wear the veil.

title: The name 'woman' belongs to the sex, not to marriage
english: But since they seize upon the name “woman” in such a way that they think it belongs only to one who has experienced a man, we must prove that the proper force of that word belongs to the sex itself, not to a degree of the sex, so that virgins are also commonly counted under it. When this second kind of human being was made by God as a helper for man, that female was immediately named woman—still blessed, still worthy of paradise, still a virgin. “She shall be called woman,” Scripture says (Genesis 2:23). So you have a name that I do not say is merely common to a virgin, but proper to her, which a virgin received from the beginning.

But some cleverly want this to have been said about the future: “She shall be called woman,” as if she would become this when she had unsealed her virginity, since Scripture also added, “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and will be joined to his woman, and the two will be in one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Let them first show where this subtlety lies: if she was named woman with reference to the future, what name did she receive in the meantime? For she could not have been without a name for her present condition. What kind of reasoning is it that one who would be called by a designated name in the future was called nothing in the present? Adam gave names to all the animals, and to none of them from a future condition, but from their present constitution; whatever condition might serve it, each was called what he willed from the beginning. What then was she called at that time?

But every time she is named in Scripture, she is called woman before she is married, and never virgin, even though she was a virgin. This name was her only one then, and it was not spoken in a prophetic manner. For when Scripture reports that the two were naked, Adam and his woman (Genesis 2:25), this does not have a future sense, as if it called her his woman as a foretelling of a wife, but because she was also his woman while unmarried, since she came from his own substance. “This,” he says, “is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; she shall be called woman” (Genesis 2:23). From this, then, the soul’s own divinity, through nature’s silent awareness, brought this usage into common speech without people knowing it—as with many other things that we can show elsewhere are customarily done and said from Scripture—so that we call our women wives, although we also speak some things improperly. For the Greeks too, who use the word for woman more often for a wife, have other proper words for wife. But I prefer to count this usage as testimony from Scripture.

For where two are made into one flesh through the bond of marriage, flesh from flesh and bone from bones is called, according to origin, his woman, from whose substance she begins to be reckoned as having become a wife. Thus woman is not by nature the name of a wife, but wife is by condition the name of a woman. In short, a woman can be called woman and not wife, but one who is not a woman cannot be called a wife, because she cannot be one So when the name of the new female was established—which is woman—and what was prior was made explicit, that is, the assigned name, he now turns to the prophetic reasoning, so as to say, “On account of her a man will leave his father and mother” (Genesis 2:24). The name is so separate from the prophecy, as much as from the person herself, that he did not speak about Eve herself, but about those future females whom he named in the womb of the female race. Otherwise Adam was not going to leave a father and mother, whom he did not have, because of Eve. Therefore what was said prophetically does not pertain to Eve, because it does not pertain to Adam either. It was foretold about the condition of husbands, who would leave their parents because of a woman—which could not fall upon Eve, because it could not fall upon Adam.

If this is so, it is clear that she was not named woman on account of a future which did not pertain to her. To this is added the fact that he himself gave the reason for her name. For when he had said, “She shall be called woman,” he said, “because she was taken from her man” (Genesis 2:23)—and he himself was still a virgin. But we will speak about the man’s name in its proper place. Let no one, then, interpret the name as prophecy, since it was derived from another meaning, especially when it is clear where she received a name from the future—there, of course, where she is named Eve, now with a personal name, because the natural one had preceded. For if Eve is the mother of the living (Genesis 3:20), behold, she is named from the future; behold, she is foretold as a wife and not a virgin. This will be the name of one about to marry; for from a married woman comes a mother. So here too it is shown that she was not then named woman from the future, since she would later receive the name of her future condition. This answer is sufficient for that part.
orientation: Tertullian is answering opponents who claim the word 'woman' applies only to a married woman, and he is proving from Genesis that Eve was called 'woman' while still a virgin.

title: Paul and Gabriel call Mary 'woman' while she is still a virgin
english: Let us now see whether the apostle also follows the pattern of this word according to Genesis, assigning it to the female sex, calling the virgin Mary a woman just as Genesis calls Eve one. Writing to the Galatians, he says, “God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Galatians 4:4). And she was certainly a virgin, even if the heretic Hebion resists that claim.

I recognize too that the angel Gabriel was sent to a virgin. But when he blesses her, he reckons her among women, not among virgins: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28). The angel also knew that even a virgin is called a woman.

But someone has thought he answered these two points cleverly: since Mary was betrothed, she was therefore pronounced a woman by both the angel and the apostle. For a betrothed woman is in some way married. Yet there is a great difference between “in some way” and “truly,” at least in this place. Elsewhere it may be taken so. But here they did not pronounce Mary a woman as if she were already married, but as nonetheless female, even if not a bride, as one called this from the beginning. For that original pattern must determine the matter from which the form descends.

As for this point, if a betrothed woman is made equal to a married one, so that Mary was called a woman not because she was female but because she was married, then Christ was not born of a virgin, because he was born of a betrothed woman who had ceased to be a virgin by this name. But if he was born of a virgin, though also betrothed, yet untouched, then recognize that even a virgin, even an untouched one, is called a woman.

Here certainly nothing can seem to have been said prophetically, as if the apostle named her a future woman, that is, a married one, by saying “made from a woman.” For he could not name a later woman from whom Christ was not to be born, that is, one who had known a man. He named the one who was present, who was a virgin and was called a woman according to the proper meaning of this word, according to the pattern of the beginning, and so this meaning is defended for the virgin and for the whole race of women.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the word 'woman' in Scripture includes virgins, and now turns to the apostle Paul and the angel Gabriel as witnesses.

title: The Apostle's Reasons for Veiling Apply to Virgins
english: Let us now turn to the reasons the apostle gives for teaching that a woman ought to be veiled, and ask whether those same reasons apply to virgins as well. If they do, then the shared meaning of the word between virgins and non-virgins is established, since the same causes for the veil are found in both groups.
If the head of the woman is the man, then certainly the head of the virgin is the man too, for the married woman is made from a virgin. Unless a virgin is some monstrous third kind with its own head.

If it is shameful for a woman to be shaved or shorn, then certainly it is shameful for a virgin as well. Let the world that rivals God see to it, then, if it falsely claims that cut hair is becoming to a virgin, just as it has also permitted it for a boy. Therefore the one for whom it is equally unfitting to be shaved or shorn is equally fitting to be covered.
If the woman is the glory of the man, how much more the virgin, who is also a glory to herself? If the woman is from the man and for the sake of the man, that rib of Adam was first a virgin.
If the woman ought to have power over her head, then by even greater right the virgin ought to have it, for what is at issue belongs to her.

For if it is because of the angels—those whom we read fell from God and from heaven because of desire for women—who can presume that such angels desired bodies already defiled and the remnants of human lust, rather than that they burned more for virgins, whose flower even excuses human lust?

For Scripture also suggests this: "And it happened," it says, "when human beings began to multiply on the earth, and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw the daughters of human beings, that they were beautiful, and took wives for themselves from all whom they chose" (Genesis 6:1-2).

Here the Greek word for women implies wives, because the mention is of marriage. So when it says "daughters of human beings," it clearly points to virgins, who would still be counted as belonging to their parents—for married women are called by their husbands' names—since it could have said "wives of human beings." Likewise it does not call the angels adulterers but husbands, while they take as wives the daughters of human beings, whom it said above were born, thus also indicating virgins. Above, born; here, married to angels. I know them as nothing other than born and then married.

So dangerous a face ought to be shadowed, a face that has hurled scandals all the way to heaven, so that as she stands before God, to whom she is answerable for the angels who were driven out, she may also blush before the other angels, and may restrain that evil liberty of her head, no longer to be offered even to the eyes of men.
But even if those angels had desired women already defiled, virgins ought all the more to be veiled because of the angels, inasmuch as the angels could have sinned all the more because of virgins.

And if the apostle adds also the judgment of nature, that a woman's honor is the abundance of her hair, because the hair is given as a covering, then certainly this is especially the mark of virgins, whose very adornment is properly such that, piled up on the crown, it covers the very citadel of the head with a circling mass of hair.
orientation: Tertullian is now reviewing the apostle Paul's arguments for why a woman must be veiled, to show that each reason applies equally to virgins.

title: The apostle's silence about virgins means they are included in 'woman'
english: All these things, of course, produce the opposite for the man, so that he does not veil his head: because he has not naturally acquired a love of hair-display; because it is not shameful for him to be shaved or shorn; because the angels did not go astray on his account; because he is the glory and image of God; because Christ is his head (1 Corinthians 11:7, 3). So when the apostle discusses the man and the woman, why she ought to be veiled and he not, it is clear why he was also silent about the virgin: he allowed the virgin to be understood in the word 'woman' by the same reasoning by which he did not name the boy, since the boy is to be counted under 'man.' He embraced the whole order of each sex with its proper terms, 'woman' and 'man.' Thus Adam, still untouched, is called 'man' in Genesis: 'She shall be called woman,' he says, 'because she was taken from her man' (Genesis 2:23). So Adam was a man before the union of marriage, just as Eve was a woman. On both sides the apostle pronounced sufficiently for the whole class of each sex, and briefly and fully, with so complete a definition: 'Every woman,' he says (1 Corinthians 11:5). What is 'every' but of every kind, of every order, of every condition, of every rank, of every age? For 'every' is whole and complete and lacking no part of itself. And the virgin is a part of 'woman.' Likewise about the man not being veiled, he says 'Every' (1 Corinthians 11:4). See the two different names, man and woman. 'Every' applies to each. Two laws bound to each other: on one side veiling, on the other uncovering. Therefore, if because it says 'every man,' the name 'man' is common also to one not yet a man, a male not yet of age—and since the name is common according to nature, the law of not veiling is also common to him who is a virgin among men according to discipline—why should it not likewise be decided beforehand that every virgin woman is contained in the name 'woman' by the sharing of the name, so that she is contained also in the common law? If a virgin is not a woman, then a male not yet of age is not a man. If a virgin is not covered because she is not a woman, then let the male not yet of age be covered because he is not a man. Let the same virginity receive equal allowance. Just as virgins are not compelled to be veiled, so boys should not be ordered to be uncovered. Why do we recognize the apostle's definition as complete on one side, regarding every man, and do not question why he did not name the boy, yet on the other side we transgress, when it is equally complete regarding every woman? 'If anyone is contentious,' he says, 'we have no such custom, nor do the churches of God' (1 Corinthians 11:16). He shows that there had been some contention about this matter, to extinguish which he used the whole summary: not naming the virgin, to show that her being veiled is not to be doubted, and naming 'every woman' as though he had named the virgin. The Corinthians themselves understood it this way. In fact, to this day the Corinthians veil their virgins. What the apostles taught, those who learned from them confirm.
orientation: Tertullian is explaining why Paul's rule that men must not be veiled but women must be veiled applies equally to virgins, even though Paul did not name virgins explicitly.

title: No privilege of place or office for virgins
english: Let us now see whether, just as we have shown that the arguments from nature and from causes apply to the virgin as well, the rules of church discipline about women also look to the virgin. A woman is not permitted to speak in church, nor to teach, nor to baptize, nor to offer the Eucharist, nor to claim for herself the lot of any manly function, much less of priestly office. Let us ask whether any of these things is allowed to a virgin. If it is not allowed to a virgin, but she is subjected in all things under the same condition, and the necessity of humility is reckoned to her along with the woman, whence will this one thing be allowed to her which is not allowed to every female? What prerogative does she deserve against her own condition, if she is a virgin and has proposed to sanctify her flesh? Is exemption from the veil granted her for this reason, so that she may enter the church notable and distinguished, so that she may display the honor of sanctity in the freedom of her head? She could have been honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office.

I know well that somewhere a virgin has been placed in the order of widows before the age of twenty. If the bishop owed her any refreshment, he could certainly have provided it in another way while preserving respect for discipline, so that such a miracle, I should not say monster, would not be marked out in the church: a virgin widow, all the more portentous because she did not cover her head even as a widow, denying both that she is a virgin who is counted as a widow, and that she is a widow who is called a virgin. But she sits there unveiled by the same authority as a virgin, and to that seat, beyond sixty years of age, not only married women are sometimes chosen, but also mothers, and indeed those who have raised children, so that, built up by experiences of all affections, they may easily know how to help other women with counsel and comfort, and so that they may have run through those things by which a woman can be tested. So nothing at all is permitted to a virgin for honor from that place.
orientation: Tertullian has shown that nature and the reasons for veiling apply to virgins; he now turns to church discipline, asking whether any of the things forbidden to women are allowed to virgins.

title: No insignia for virgins if men lack them
english: So it is not with any other marks of distinction. It would be quite inhuman if women, who are subjected to men in everything, were to display the honor-bearing mark of their virginity, by which they are looked up to, noticed, and praised by the brothers, while men—so many virgins, so many voluntary eunuchs—walk about with their own good hidden, carrying nothing that would make them distinguished too. For they would have to claim some insignia for themselves as well: the feathers of the Garamantes, the headbands of the barbarians, the cicadas of the Athenians, the hair-knots of the Germans, or the tattoos of the Britons. Or let the opposite happen: let them hide in church with veiled heads.

We are certain that the Holy Spirit could more readily have prescribed something like this for males, if He had prescribed it for females, since apart from the authority of sex, males ought rather to be honored in the very name of continence. The more eager and hot their sex is toward women, the greater and more laborious their continence is, and therefore the more worthy of every display—if display of virginity is a dignity. Does not continence rank above virginity, whether that of widowers or of those who by mutual consent have already refused the common insult? For virginity consists of grace, but continence of virtue. It is a great struggle not to desire what you have grown accustomed to desiring. But when you have never known the fruit of desire, you will easily not desire it, since you have no adversary—the desire for the fruit. How then would God not more readily have prescribed something like this for men in their honor, either because they are closer to His own image, or because they labor more? But if nothing was prescribed for the male, much less for the female.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that virgins deserve no special marks of honor, since men who practice continence receive none.

title: Maturity, not birth, begins the obligation of the veil
english: But let me now settle the point I passed over earlier, so as not to break the thread of the argument. When I established from the apostle's absolute definition that every woman of every age must be understood, the objection from the other side was that a virgin would then have to be veiled from birth and from the first name of her age. But that is not how it is. She must be veiled from the time she begins to understand herself, to enter into the awareness of her own nature, to leave the state of virginity, and to suffer that new thing which belongs to another age. For Adam and Eve, the first parents of our race, went about naked as long as they lacked understanding. But when they tasted from the tree of knowledge, the first thing they felt was that they must be ashamed, and so each marked the understanding of their own sex with a covering.

But even if a woman must be veiled because of the angels, the law of the veil will without doubt take effect from the age at which the daughters of men could draw desire to themselves and undergo marriage. For a virgin ceases to be a virgin from the moment she is able not to be one. That is why among Israel it is unlawful to hand a girl over to a man until her maturity has been attested by blood; before that sign she is considered unripe. So if she is a virgin as long as she is unripe, she ceases to be a virgin when she is recognized as mature, and since she is no longer a virgin she is subject to the law, just as she is to marriage.

Betrothed women have the example of Rebecca. When she was being led to a bridegroom still unknown to her, herself still unknown to him, the moment she recognized that he was the one she had seen from afar, she did not endure the clasping of his right hand, nor the meeting of a kiss, nor the sharing of a greeting. Instead she confessed what she had felt—that she was already a bride in spirit—and by veiling herself on the spot she denied that she was a virgin. What a woman already instructed in the discipline of Christ! She showed that even marriage happens through sight and mind, just as adultery does—except that some people still veil Rebecca herself.

As for the rest, those who are not betrothed, let the parents' delay, born of narrow circumstances or scrupulosity, be their concern; let the vow of continence itself be their concern. None of this has anything to do with age, which runs its own course and pays its own debts to maturity. Another mother in secret, nature, and another father in hiding, time, have married their daughter by their own laws. Look at that virgin of yours: she is already married—her soul by expectation, her flesh by transformation—for whom you are preparing a second husband. Her voice has already deepened, her limbs have filled out, modesty clothes her everywhere, her months pay their tribute—and you deny that she is a woman, when you admit she suffers a woman's things?

If union with a man makes a woman, then let no one be veiled until after the actual experience of marriage. But even among the pagans, women are veiled when they are led to their husbands. If they are veiled at betrothal, because they have been joined to a male in body and spirit through the kiss and the right hands—through which they first unsealed their modesty in spirit, through the common pledge of conscience by which they pledged all their shame—how much more will time veil them, without which they cannot be betrothed, and under whose pressure virgins cease to be virgins even without betrothal?

Even the pagans observe time, so that by the law of nature they render to each age its own rights. They send girls out to business at twelve years old, and boys two years later, determining puberty by years, not by betrothals or marriages. A girl is called mother of a family, even if she is a virgin; a boy is called father of a family, even if he is still beardless. Among us not even the natural things are observed, as if the God of nature were different from ours.
orientation: Tertullian is answering an objection to his earlier argument that the apostle's word 'woman' includes every age, and he now explains that the veil becomes obligatory when a girl reaches the age of self-understanding and sexual maturity.

title: Age itself testifies to womanhood
english: Recognize the woman, and recognize the bride, by the testimony of both body and spirit, by what she endures in conscience and in flesh. These are the earlier records of natural betrothals and marriages. Put the veil on outwardly, since she has a covering inwardly. Let the upper parts be covered too, since the lower parts are not bare. Do you want to know the authority of age? Set both before you: one changed by defloration into a woman's dress, and one who has advanced in maturity and remains in virginity with her own dress. The first will more easily be denied to be a woman than the second will be believed to be a virgin. So great is the testimony of age that not even dress can block it. What then? Even these women of ours confess the change of age by their dress, and as soon as they understand themselves to be women, they are brought out from among the virgins, removing from their heads the sign of what they were. They turn their hair and pin it up with a more wanton pin, parting the hair from the forehead and openly professing womanhood. They soak themselves in the bath, seek beauty from the mirror, and make their face more fastidious by washing, perhaps even touching it up with some cosmetic. They fling a mantle over themselves, cram their feet into elaborate shoes, and carry more equipment to the baths. Why should I pursue every detail? Their visible preparations alone carry their whole womanhood around with them, yet they want to be virgins by the bareness of the head alone, denying with one garment what they profess with their whole display.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that a virgin's own body and conduct testify that she is a woman, so she should accept the veil.

title: Veiling before God, not for human praise
english: If they misuse their dress for the sake of men, let them carry that through here as well: just as they veil their heads among the pagans, let them at least hide their virginity in the church, since they hide it outside the church. They fear strangers; let them also respect their brothers and sisters. Or let them be bold enough to appear as virgins in the streets, just as they dare to do in the churches. I will praise their vigor if they have marketed anything of their virginity even among the pagans. The same nature exists outside as inside; the same practice holds among men and before the Lord with the same freedom. Why, then, do they hide away their good outside but publish it in the church? I demand a reason. Is it to please their brothers, or to please God Himself? If it is to please God Himself, He is as able to see whatever is done in secret as He is just in rewarding what is done for Him alone. In fact, He commands that we should not trumpet any of the things that will earn a reward from Him, and that we should not have them repaid by men. If we are forbidden to let the left hand know about a single penny's worth of almsgiving, or any act of charity at all, how much darkness should we pour around ourselves when we offer God so great an offering as our very body and our very spirit, when we consecrate our very nature to Him? Therefore, what cannot be seen to be done for God's sake—because God does not want it done that way—follows as being done for human favor, which is certainly unlawful in the first place, as lustful for glory. For glory is unlawful for those whose testing consists in every kind of humiliation. And if the virtue of continence is given by God, why do you glory as if you had not received it? But if you have not received it, what do you have that was not given to you? By this very fact it is clear that it was not given to you by God, because you do not offer it to God alone. Let us see, then, whether what is human is firm and true.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing virgins who go unveiled in church, arguing that if they hide their virginity from outsiders they should hide it from fellow Christians too, since God alone should see what is done for him.

title: The ruin that follows from virgins seeking glory
english: They report that someone once said, when this question was first raised, "And how shall we solicit the rest to this kind of work?" Of course they will make us happy if there are more of them, and not by God's grace or each one's merits. Do virgins adorn the church to God, or does the church adorn virgins, or commend them? He confessed, then, that glory is at stake. Moreover, where there is glory, there is solicitation; where solicitation, compulsion; where compulsion, necessity; where necessity, weakness. Rightly, therefore, while they do not cover their heads in order to be solicited for the sake of glory, they are compelled to cover their bellies by the ruin of weakness. For rivalry, not religion, brings them out.

Sometimes even their own belly is swollen tight, because the brotherhood readily receives virgins. Nor do they merely fall, but they also drag after themselves a long rope of sins. For when they are brought out into public and lifted up by the publicizing of their good, and heaped up by the brothers with every honor and work of love, while they do not fall, when something has been committed, they think of as much disgrace as they had honor.

If an uncovered head is ascribed to virginity, if any virgin falls from the grace of virginity, lest she be exposed, she remains with uncovered head, and then she walks in a habit that is not her own. Conscious now of undoubted womanhood, they dare to approach God with bare head. But God is a jealous God and Lord, who said, "Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed" (Matthew 10:26), and He brings very many even into public view. For they will not confess unless betrayed by the wailings of their own infants. But the more numerous they are, will you not also suspect them of more crimes? I will say it, though I do not wish to: a woman who fears becoming one hardly becomes one only once, and she who has already become one can lie that she is a virgin under God.

How much will she dare concerning her own womb, lest she also be exposed as a mother? God knows how many infants He has helped to be both completed and brought to birth whole, after being fought against for some time by their mothers. Such virgins always conceive most easily and give birth most happily, and indeed to children most like their fathers. Coerced and unwilling virginity admits these disgraceful acts. The very desire not to hide is not modest. She suffers something that is not a virgin's—the eagerness to please, certainly, even men. However much she may strive with good intention, she must be endangered by the publicizing of herself, while she is struck by uncertain and many eyes, while she is titillated by the fingers of those pointing her out, while she is loved too much, while she grows warm amid embraces and constant kisses. Thus the brow is hardened, thus modesty is worn away, thus she is loosened, thus she learns to desire to please in another way.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that veiling virgins will discourage others from embracing virginity, and he now traces the moral ruin that comes when virgins go unveiled for the sake of glory.

title: True virginity fears itself and hides
english: But true, complete, and pure virginity fears nothing more than itself. It refuses to endure even the eyes of women; it has eyes of its own. It flees for refuge to the veil of the head as to a helmet, as to a shield, to protect its good against the blows of temptations, against the darts of scandals, against suspicions and whispers and rivalry, and against envy itself. For there is something to be feared even among the pagans which they call the evil eye, a most unhappy outcome of excessive praise and glory. We sometimes interpret this as the devil, since hatred of good belongs to him; sometimes we attribute it to God, since judgment of pride belongs to Him, who exalts the humble and casts down the proud. Therefore the holier virgin will fear, even in the name of the evil eye, the adversary on one side and God on the other—the one's spiteful nature, the other's censoring light—and she will rejoice to be known to herself alone and to God. But even if she becomes known to someone, she is wise if she bars the way against temptations. For who will dare to press with his eyes upon a closed face, a face not feeling, a face, so to speak, sad? Every evil thought will be broken by that very severity. Now she who conceals a virgin denies that she is even a woman.
orientation: Tertullian is describing how a true virgin protects her modesty by veiling, after arguing that unveiled virgins are endangered by public attention.

title: Scripture, nature, and discipline all demand the veil
english: Here lies the defense of our position: according to Scripture, according to nature, according to discipline. Scripture establishes the law, nature bears witness, discipline demands it. Which of these does a custom of opinion benefit, or what gives color to a contrary view? Scripture is God's, nature is God's, discipline is God's. Whatever is contrary to these is not God's. If Scripture is uncertain, nature is clear, and from nature's testimony Scripture cannot be uncertain. If there is doubt about nature, discipline shows what God has ratified more fully. Nothing is dearer to Him than humility, nothing more acceptable than modesty, nothing more burdensome than glory and the desire to please men. So let whatever you find ratified by God be for you Scripture and nature and discipline, just as you are commanded to examine everything and follow what is better. It remains for me to turn to the virgins themselves, so that they may receive these things more willingly. I ask you—whether mother, sister, or virgin daughter, to use the names of your years—veil your head. If you are a mother, for your sons; if a sister, for your brothers; if a daughter, for your fathers. Every age is endangered in you. Put on the armor of modesty, raise a rampart of modesty, build a wall for your sex that neither lets out your own eyes nor admits the eyes of others. Fulfill the dress of a woman, so that you may preserve the state of a virgin. Feign something of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone. Yet you are not feigning that you are married. You have married Christ; to Him you have handed over your flesh, to Him you have betrothed your maturity. Walk according to your bridegroom's will. It is Christ who commands both other men's brides and married women to be veiled—how much more His own.
orientation: Tertullian is concluding his argument by grounding the veiling of virgins in Scripture, nature, and discipline, then directly exhorting virgins to veil themselves.

title: Exhortation to veiled women and final warning
english: But we also warn you, women of another modesty, you who have fallen into marriage: do not grow old away from the discipline of the veil, not even for a moment of an hour. Because you cannot reject it outright, do not destroy it in another way, going about neither covered nor bare. For with headbands and woolen wraps some do not veil the head but bind it up, protected at the forehead, but bare where the head properly is. Others are covered with small linen cloths, I suppose so as not to press the head, and not even let down to the ears, but covered only as far as the crown of the head. I pity them if their hearing is so weak that they cannot hear through a covering. Let them know that the whole head is woman. Its limits and boundaries extend as far as where the clothing begins. As much space as loosened hair can occupy, so much is the region of the veil, so that the neck too is encircled. For these are what must be subjected, and because of them authority must be held over the head. The veil is their yoke.

The pagan women of Arabia will judge you, who cover not the head but the whole face as well, so that with one eye left free they are content to enjoy half the light rather than to prostitute the whole face. A woman prefers to see than to be seen. A certain Roman queen said that they are most unhappy for this reason, because they can love more than be loved, when in fact they are happy through immunity from another and indeed more common unhappiness, because women can more easily be loved than love. And indeed the modesty of pagan discipline is purer and, so to speak, more barbarous.

For us the Lord has measured out the extent of the veil even through revelations. For to a certain sister of ours an angel in a dream, striking her neck as if applauding, said, "Elegant neck, and rightly bare! It is good for you to be unveiled from the head down to the loins, lest this freedom of the neck fail to benefit you as well." And certainly what he said to one, he said to all.

But how much chastisement will those also deserve who persist uncovered during the psalms or at any mention of God, and who, lingering even in prayer itself, most easily place a fringe or a bit of wool or some thread on the crown of the head and think themselves covered? They lie about their head to such a degree. Others, for whom the palm is clearly greater than any fringe or thread, abuse their head no less, like a certain beast rather than a bird, winged indeed, but with a small head and outstretched neck, walking tall on long legs. They say that when it must hide, it hides only its whole head in the thicket and leaves the rest of itself in the open. So while it is secure in its head, it is caught naked where it is larger, all of it together with the head. Such will those women be who are covered less than is useful.

Therefore women must walk at every time and in every place mindful of the law, ready and prepared for every mention of God, who, if he is in the heart, will be recognized also in the head of women. May peace and grace from our Lord Jesus abound, with good peace to those who read and who prefer usefulness to custom, along with Septimius Tertullian, whose little work this is.
orientation: Tertullian is closing the treatise by exhorting married women to keep the veil at all times, warning against half-coverings, and ending with a blessing.
